title: Identity treated as explanation, yet the boxed-share fall is the very adaptation channel
quote: an identity, not a test, which does not
explanation: r_t = r_boxed x (boxed share) is an algebraic decomposition that holds under every hypothesis, adaptation or not, so it cannot 'account for' the fall; it only re-expresses it. Worse, the only way a policy can escape the gold-storage defect on a problem with parseable gold is to stop writing \boxed there, so a falling boxed share is precisely the mechanism by which adaptation would show up. Attributing the fall to the share and then calling it 'no evidence of adaptation' treats the main adaptation route as a nuisance factor. The honest reading is that the data do not identify non-selective unboxing (generic SFT damage, shorter/capped outputs) versus selective avoidance; 'accounted for' overstates, and the evidence is the (weak) r_boxed term, whose intervals (about +-3) contain the whole fall.

title: r_boxed 'flat' is not a usable reference: the gold arm shows r_boxed drifting by as much as the effect
quote: rt drifts as much as the falls we observe
explanation: The argument needs r_boxed to be a stable quantity so that the fall can be assigned to the boxed share. But the train-on-gold arms (no verifier in the loop) move r_boxed by +2.8 and +1.7, comparable to the self-training changes (-0.4 to +0.7 on boxed, -1.5 to -2.6 overall). Together with intervals of +-3 this means r_boxed's change is unresolved in both directions; the decomposition cannot be closed. Also, the denominator (V'-accepted set) changes composition as accuracy falls, which moves r_t independent of both factors; neither a composition-adjusted nor a fixed-problem-set version is reported.

title: 'Affected, parseable' subset is defined by the outcome and regresses to the mean
quote: problems where some form could, rt moves by −5.5, −1.6 and −0.2 points
explanation: The subset (problems where the defect 'ever fires') is selected using the same generations in which r_t is later measured; a problem enters only if a boxed correct answer was produced and rejected in some round. This conditioning forces r_t on this subset near its ceiling at round 0 (92-95%) and makes later values fall back by construction (regression to the mean), independent of any learning. Likewise the headline 'rejects 94-98% of correct answers in every round' on problems where it ever fires is a selection-induced rate, not an estimate of the defect's per-problem hit rate. A subset fixed from round 0 only, or from an independent sample, is needed.
related_sections: 3.2 The Verifier and Its Directional Bias

title: The studied 'verifier bias' is a harness integration defect, yet conclusions are framed about rule-based verifiers
quote: so a correct boxed prediction can fail against a bare gold
explanation: The dominant defect arises because the authors store the gold without delimiters; math-verify used as documented (gold parsed with delimiters) would not exhibit it, and V' is simply the correct call. The 29-34 of 54-62 affected problems with unparseable gold are a different cause (parser limits) folded into the same count. The title question ('Mathematics or the Verifier?'), the RLVR framing, and the claim that bias in 'a rule-based verifier' was studied overreach: the experiment shows what a mis-wired pipeline does, not what verifier bias does. The 4.7-8.0 point pass@1 'cost' is a scoring artefact of the defect, not evidence of biased selection pressure, and V' itself has no false-accept check (only rejections were audited).
source_section: 3.2 The Verifier and Its Directional Bias

title: Gate failure is read as 'null belongs to this recipe', but the failed control makes the null uninformative
quote: gate failed, the null belongs to this recipe
explanation: A positive control that fails shows that the experiment cannot discriminate a gain from no gain; the logical consequence is that the null is uninformative about the recipe, not that it is a finding about the recipe. The paper's own gate text says the recipe 'cannot be called corrected' and the failure may be a pipeline defect. If the pipeline is defective, the loop's null inherits that defect. Scoping the claim to 'this recipe' then converts an inconclusive experiment into a recipe-specific negative. The scope restriction is a hedge on generality, not a licence to call the result a null for the recipe; the title 'A Null Result for One Recipe' presupposes that the recipe was fairly tested.

title: Gate failure is plausibly a measurement artefact of the grader, and gold SFT is not a valid positive control for an instruct model
quote: That style carries no \boxed answer, which both graders read,
explanation: The prompt requires \boxed; the gold arm teaches $-delimited reference style with no \boxed, and both graders only read \boxed. A model trained this way scores near zero regardless of mathematical competence, so the -32 point 'collapse' may simply be unscorable output (the authors note both graders depend on \boxed but do not grade by last $-span / last number). Separately, off-policy terse reference solutions are not expected to raise accuracy of an already-instruction-tuned model (the cited Kim et al. result is that such SFT can lower it), whereas the loop trains on on-policy samples; so the gate may not be a positive control for the loop at all. In either case the failed gate does not bear on whether the self-generated-data arm could help, and the 'recipe passes if gate passes' criterion is unjustified. Earlier 1e-5/k=8 runs (Table 2, the bulk of the evidence) never had a gate at their settings; the 5e-4 gold arms came with different loss/targets.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Revised Recipe

title: No filter-free/random-data control in the final round: loop decline cannot be separated from generic SFT damage, yet is hedged inconsistently
quote: it costs accuracy, and we did not isolate the cause
explanation: All three loop seeds fall and the t-interval [-6.1,-2.1] excludes zero, yet the text refuses to claim a cost. The simplest alternative explanation (any SFT under this pipeline lowers accuracy: repetition penalty, fp16, unmasked or capped formats, style shift) is untested because the final round has no no-filter or shuffled-label arm; the gate failing in the same pipeline points the same way. The paper therefore cannot distinguish 'verifier-filtered self-training does not help' from 'this training stack harms', which is what 'null belongs to the recipe' needs to settle but cannot. Also inconsistent standards: a CI excluding zero is discounted here, whereas intervals that exclude zero are used to support the 5.5-10.6 finished-accuracy loss at 5e-4.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Revised Recipe

title: Cap-share decomposition is unstable and non-unique, but is promoted to a headline finding
quote: attributes 12–30% of the decline to the cap share in the three original seed-1
explanation: The cap share ranges from -2% to 72% across runs, i.e. the decomposition does not replicate and its sign changes; yet the contribution list and introduction present 'lower accuracy on the solutions the model does finish' as what 'appears most clearly'. A three-part decomposition with an interaction term has an order-dependent apportionment, so the percentages are not uniquely defined. The matched measure conditions on which problems finish post-training (selection into the finished set), which the paper concedes is only descriptive, and the cap-hit proxy (re-tokenised >=508) is approximate. With 40-50% of generations already capped at baseline and 24-26% of training examples truncated of their final answer and EOS, the cap may also be the cause of finished-accuracy loss (training on truncated, answer-less targets), not a separable component. Same-seed A/B pairs are replicates and B-A flips +5.3 to -7.3 from 0-3 example differences, so interval-based claims at problem level understate run-to-run variance.

title: 'Finished accuracy carries the whole change' at lower rates rests on point estimates whose intervals include zero
quote: At 10−4 and 2 × 10−4 the cap-hit share does not
explanation: The claim that the cap share plays no role at 1e-4 and 2e-4 is drawn from cap-hit shares at round 2 only; Table 2's matched column at those rates is mostly consistent with zero (e.g. -4.3 [-9.6,1.1], -3.5 [-9.2,2.3], -0.6 [-6.0,4.7]). Sample accuracy falls 3-4 points at 1e-4 and 5e-4 seed 2 alike (3.7 vs 4.7) while cap-hit share differs; this shows the decline is not explained by the cap share, but also that the rate-dependence of the 5e-4 'finished-accuracy' loss is not established. The narrative of a rate-driven, finished-accuracy decline mixes a well-supported seed-1 pattern with a flat seed-2 pattern.

title: Pooled-vs-isolated confound list is incomplete; 'absent in isolated runs' is overstated
quote: decline is absent in the isolated runs at 10−5,
explanation: The paper names dose and pooling, but Design P also differs in: evaluation on the selection problems themselves (selection == eval, so lost problems drop out of the pool and the pool shrinks as a function of what is evaluated), no held-out set, two datasets with very different solution lengths (Run C alone declines 12.7), a 0.5B/1.5B pair, and an accelerating pool-shrinkage feedback that the isolated runs, with a separate exam, cannot reproduce. Isolated runs do decline (pass@1 -2.7 to -12.7 at 1e-5, up to -22 on GSM8K at 5e-4), so 'absent' is a statement about magnitude only. The shrinking-pool hypothesis is also said to be neither supported nor ruled out, yet the no-filter arm (constant pool) declines too, which actually argues the shrinkage is not necessary for decline. No dose-matched isolated run exists (they could have trained Run A at 5e-4 for 5 rounds on the pooled dose), so the confound is never reduced.

title: Injected-bias controls: content rule is 'visible' only in the gold, not to the model, and a one-round test cannot calibrate multi-round adaptation
quote: every \boxed answer is rejected when the gold contains \frac
explanation: The model sees the problem, not the gold, so the rule is learnable only insofar as problem text predicts a \frac gold. Moreover the control runs a single adapter on 49 penalised problems for one round at k=2, while the real audit spans several rounds, a different dose (2-12 avoidance examples) and a different penalty (a rejected correct answer, not a blanket rule). The negative result (+2.8 in the wrong direction) is thus evidence that this setting does not elicit avoidance at all, which is itself informative about the expected adaptation to the real defect (probably none), yet the paper says both are uninformative and 'expects weak pressure (untested)'. The framing as 'intended positive controls' that 'turn out not to be' is therefore too pessimistic in one place and the audit's detectability remains unquantified in another.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Revised Recipe

title: Null-for-gains is asserted with no equivalence test while point estimates are consistently negative
quote: Not detectably. No run raises pass@1
explanation: 'Not detectably' is a power-limited statement (about 10 points at 150 problems, 6 at 500), not support for a null; the design could not rule out gains of 8-10 points and, for pass@1, almost all estimates are negative. The paper's own bounds use h that omits training-seed variance, which it says is as large as 7 points. Calling the study 'A Null Result' and writing the conclusion around 'no gain at any rate' blends absence of evidence with evidence of absence; combined with the failed gate, the study supports neither 'self-training helps' nor 'self-training does not', yet the title and flow suggest a negative finding about the recipe.

title: Gate failure may be a measurement artefact, undermining 'null for the recipe'
quote: rule out a format artefact in the gate. Earlier runs are not independently graded.
explanation: Section 5.1 and the Conclusion argue that because the positive gate failed (49.2 -> 17.0) the null 'belongs to this recipe'. But Section 4.6 says the reference style carries no \boxed answer, which both graders read, that a collapse of this size from 300 solutions is what a pipeline defect would produce, and 5.1 concedes the independent grader does not rule out a format artefact in the gate. If the gate drop is a grading/format artefact, the gate neither validates nor invalidates the recipe, so 'this is a null for the recipe' (rather than 'the study cannot interpret the recipe at all') is not established; the conclusion needs one reading or the other. The authors honestly state the gate cannot validate the recipe, but the Conclusion still draws a positive scoping inference from it.
related_sections: 4.6 A Final Round with a Revised Recipe

title: Train-on-gold used as a 'drift' control although its accepted set is collapsed and the effect is opposite in sign
quote: so rt drifts as much as the falls we observe, unrelated to the
explanation: Table 5 gold runs rise by +3.3 and +2.1 with intervals [-1.2,8.1] and [-2.2,6.7], both including zero. Concluding that r_t 'drifts as much as the falls we observe' treats two noisy, opposite-sign changes as a noise-floor estimate. Further, the gold arms are a different regime (accuracy collapsed, outputs shift to a reference style per 4.6, so the V'-accepted set is a small, selected survivor subset whose composition and size are not reported), so they do not calibrate the sampling drift of r_t in the self-training runs. The boxed share among accepted answers implied by Table 5 even rises in gold runs (about 91% -> 94%), at odds with the stated style shift away from \boxed. Also 'unrelated to the verifier' is asserted without a matched control. The inference about drift magnitude is therefore weaker than stated; denominators (#V'-accepted per round) should be given.

title: Affected-problem counts mix exam and selection problems, overstating the adaptive-pressure set
quote: The adaptation audit is weak: 24–28 problems, 2–12
explanation: Table 5 is computed over all 500 problems with selection problems included, so the 'affected, parseable' subset (24-28 problems, intervals up to 26 wide) includes exam problems that never enter the training pool in Design I (150 of 500 are exam). Only selection problems can exert pressure to avoid the defect, yet the power statement in the Limitations and Conclusion ('about 25 affected problems') pairs this count with the pool counts (2-12 examples), which come from selection problems only. The effective number of problems that can teach avoidance is smaller (roughly 70% of 24-28), and the numerator/denominator populations of the audit and of the pressure are inconsistent. Separately, defining the subset by problems where the defect 'ever fires' (over all rounds, including the last) conditions on the outcome and can bias R0 vs last differences by regression to the mean.

title: Cap-share range reported selectively in the audit section
quote: at 5 × 10−4 the cap share accounts for 12–30% of the decline in the
explanation: Section 4.5 reports the cap share as 12-30% in three seed-1 runs, 52-72% at seed 2 and also -2% and 5% in two further runs. Section 5.3(ii) and the summary drop the -2/5% runs, so the quoted spread understates the heterogeneity (range -2% to 72%). Together with the Conclusion's flat statement that 'at the highest rate the model is less accurate on the solutions it finishes' (a post hoc, descriptive measure that conditions on which problems finish, and which at seed 2 explains under half of the decline), the headline reads stronger than the decomposition supports.

title: Conclusion states finished-accuracy loss flatly despite descriptive/post hoc status
quote: At the highest rate the model is less accurate on the solutions
explanation: Section 4.5 says the matched finished-accuracy measure conditions on which problems finish after training, so it is descriptive, and the cap-share decomposition attributes up to 52-72% of the decline at seed 2 to the cap. The Conclusion presents the finished-solution accuracy loss as a finding without the caveat or the dose/rate confound (5e-4 is the dose-heavy arm).

title: Final-round decline is consistent in sign, two graders and the mean interval, yet discussion treats it as 'not detectable'/uninterpreted
quote: loop does not help; the point estimates are negative in all three seeds,
explanation: The mean pass@1 change is -4.1 with t-interval [-6.1,-2.1] and sample accuracy -4.5 [-8.1,-1.0] (I recomputed both from the seed values; they are right), two of three per-seed pass@1 intervals exclude zero, and the independent grader agrees in sign and size. Elsewhere the paper reads intervals excluding zero as evidence; here the Discussion (5.1, 5.2) only says 'not detectably better' and declines to say the loop costs accuracy, and never uses the decline to discuss mechanisms (format drift, boxed share falling, truncation). The authors' own threshold (about 6 points) exceeds the observed 4.1, so the null framing is a power statement, but then the consistent negative direction in an under-powered design deserves explicit treatment as suggestive evidence of harm, particularly since the identity in 5.3 shows the boxed share is falling, which lowers both graders (acknowledged) and could itself explain the whole decline.
related_sections: 4.6 A Final Round with a Revised Recipe

title: Recommending r_t as a per-round audit contradicts the paper's own finding that it is non-diagnostic
quote: From post hoc analyses we propose four checks for
explanation: Section 5.3 shows the headline statistic r_t is mechanically tied to the boxed share (identity), its fall is matched by the gold control's drift, and the two injected-bias runs could not validate it ('neither can tell us whether the audit would detect it'). Proposing it as protocol (i) is framed as 'not tested methods', but the refined version (restrict to answers/problems where V and V' can differ and an accepted form exists) has not been computed with any usable power (intervals 10-26 wide) nor validated. Items (iii) and (iv) concern dose matching and are not audit checks derived from the r_t analysis. The section title and the protocol framing overstate what the data support.

title: Boxed-only interval width stated as about +-3 though one run is about +-1.6
quote: have intervals (≈±3) that contain the overall fall of the same run (−2.6, −2.6,
explanation: Table 5 boxed-only intervals are [-2.9,4.3], [-2.8,3.4] and [-2.0,1.2], i.e. half-widths about 3.6, 3.1 and 1.6. For the 1e-5 run the 'flat means not detected' argument rests on an interval whose half-width is half that stated, and the overall fall (-1.5, [-2.9,0.0]) is nearly outside it. Minor, but 'flat means not detected' should be run-specific. Also the overall-fall intervals touch zero, so the comparison 'interval contains the overall fall' does not establish equivalence.

title: Possible train/exam overlap for the 300 MATH-train pool is unchecked and absent from Limitations
quote: We report no overlap check of the 300 pool problems
explanation: The final-round pool is 300 MATH training problems evaluated on all MATH-500. No overlap or near-duplicate check is reported, and the Limitations section (which lists contamination of Qwen2.5 on MATH/GSM8K) omits this item. Overlap would inflate loop and gate accuracy in the final round, which is the paper's strongest evidence round; it should be checked or listed.
related_sections: 4.6 A Final Round with a Revised Recipe

title: Failed positive gate removes the meaning of both the null and the power statement
quote: diagnose (a pipeline defect would also produce it), so the null concerns
explanation: The paper says the gate must raise accuracy for the recipe to count as able to help; it falls 49.2 to 17.0, and the 5e-4 gold arms fall about 20-26 points. The 'detectable gain of ~10 (6) points' is therefore a statement about a pipeline that has never been shown able to register any gain. A null from an instrument with no demonstrated sensitivity is uninformative, not a null 'for the recipe'; the title and 'Null Result' framing overstate this. The authors admit the collapse could be a pipeline defect yet leave it undiagnosed, although cheap diagnostics exist (inspect gold-arm generations, regrade $-span answers, train on gold rewritten into the model's own \boxed format). Until a gate passes, the honest label is 'inconclusive / no detectable gain from an unvalidated pipeline', and the sub-claim that the result concerns the recipe presupposes the pipeline works.
related_sections: 4.6 A Final Round with a Revised Recipe

title: Gate confounded with grader: reference-style outputs carry no \boxed and both graders read \boxed
quote: That style carries no \boxed answer, which both graders read,
explanation: The gate trains on reference solutions that use $-delimited spans and no \boxed; the model adopts that style (60 to 1,577 of 1,600). Both math-verify (as used here) and the independent string-match grader read the last \boxed, so a format shift alone predicts a collapse of the size seen. The second grader therefore cannot arbitrate for the gate (-30.0 matches -32.2 by construction). The gate as built tests 'does the model keep emitting \boxed' rather than 'can this recipe improve mathematics'. A fair gate would make the positive arm use the same output format as the evaluated arms. This also asymmetrically handicaps the gold arm relative to the self-training arms, whose data are in the evaluated format, so cross-arm comparison to the gold arm is unfair.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Revised Recipe

title: Significant, consistent decline in the final round coexists with a 'null' headline and is treated asymmetrically
quote: The loop does not help; the point estimates are negative in all three seeds
explanation: The pooled loop result is -4.1 pass@1 with a t-interval [-6.1,-2.1] and -4.5 sample accuracy [-8.1,-1.0], both excluding zero (I verified the t-interval arithmetic for n=3). The paper simultaneously says 'we do not claim that it costs accuracy' and lists intervals reaching zero as 'no evidence' elsewhere. The paper states it applies 'the same reading to declines and to gains', but the abstract and title foreground 'no gain', while a replicated decline is the only reliably non-null effect in the study. Either the three-seed interval is credible (then the decline is a finding, with the gate-failure caveat) or it is not (then the paper should say what the three seeds do establish). Note also that the three seeds share one 500-problem exam draw and a common pipeline, so the t-interval omits exam-draw variance and is not the independent-replicate estimate it resembles.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Revised Recipe

title: Power analysis presented as 80% power but is optimistic, derived per-run, and ignores that the controls were never validated
quote: even with h as the whole error, a gain at that size is missed 20% of the time,
explanation: The 2.8h/1.96 rule uses the bootstrap half-width of a single run, which omits training-seed variance. The paper's own gauge (replicate pair 3.2 pts apart; B-A flipping +5.3 to -7.3; per-seed sample-accuracy swings of a few points) implies true minimum detectable effects well above 10 pts pass@1, yet the abstract, Intro and Conclusion repeat 'about 10 (6)' as the design's sensitivity, with 'likely more' in small print. The paper criticises others for ignoring seed variance (Xu et al.) but its headline sensitivity does the same; a seed-variance-inclusive estimate (e.g., pooling the 3 seeds at 1e-4 in Table 2 or the 3 final-round seeds) is available and should replace the optimistic figure. Further, pass@1 uses one sample per problem, so its detectability is far worse than that of sample accuracy, which was nevertheless chosen post hoc as primary.

title: Inconsistent sensitivity figures: 3.5-5.5 detectable vs a 2.2-point 'bound'
quote: is the largest upper limit among observed intervals
explanation: Section 3.4 says sample-accuracy gains below about 3.5-5.5 points could be missed; Section 5.1 reports a ~2.2-point figure that is the maximum of the upper limits of observed intervals. The latter is a maximum over a selected, post hoc statistic across non-independent runs, not a bound on any effect; its natural reading ('gains above 2.2 are excluded') contradicts the 3.5-5.5 detectability threshold stated earlier. Using a max-of-upper-limits is also a form of selecting the most favourable summary and, as intervals omit seed variance, understates uncertainty. It should either be removed or reconciled with the power statement.

title: Learning-rate 'grid' conflates rate with k, rounds, pool size and metric, so 'no gain at any learning rate' is not a clean claim
quote: so only 10−4 to 5 × 10−4 isolates the
explanation: The 1e-5 arm (k=8, 5 rounds, pass@8) and the 1e-4..5e-4 arms (k=4, 3 rounds, pass@4) differ in more than rate, and the final round changes seven things at once (k=2, 1 adapter, new pool, loss, LoRA targets, cap). pass@k values for different k are not comparable, and pass@1 compares a single draw. Neither is the 1e-5 arm a low-dose match of the higher-rate arms. 'No gain at any learning rate' is thus a union of non-comparable null tests, each with different sensitivity, and the headline sentence reads as a rate sweep that was not performed. The authors state the confound but still headline the conclusion at rate level; moreover the best-case design for finding a gain (more rounds at the intermediate rate with k held fixed) was not run.

title: No multiplicity or family-wise reading although the conclusion is a universal 'no gain at any rate'
quote: We make no multiplicity correction and the runs are not independent (they share
explanation: The central claim 'No pass@1 or pass@k gain has an interval excluding zero' is effectively an intersection null over ~20 runs x 4 metrics, while many cells share exam partitions and round-0 draws. Not correcting is conservative for a claim of 'no gain' (it makes false positives more likely), but the paper then uses uncorrected 95% intervals to highlight subsets that do exclude zero (5e-4 decline in 'four A/B runs', 'five of six' matched intervals) and builds the 'lower accuracy on finished solutions' headline on them. The treatment is inconsistent: multiplicity is waved away in the null direction yet the same uncorrected intervals support the one positive claim in the abstract/Introduction. The 'descriptive not tests' disclaimer does not stop these being headline claims.

title: Dose-response reading from two seeds sits inside the paper's own noise floor
quote: at seed 1 sample accuracy falls 1.5, 3.5 and 8.3 points
explanation: The paper says a replicate pair differs by 3.2 points and B-A flips by 12.6 points, then describes a rate-dependent decline ('may grow with the rate on one seed') and an 'appears most clearly at the highest rate' headline. With seed 2 flat (3.7, 3.8, 4.7) and intervals per cell +/-3-4, one seed trend is not distinguishable from trajectory noise; the seed that supports the claim also determines the exam partition. The matched 'finished accuracy' measure that gives the highest-rate result conditions on post-training outcomes (the authors say it is descriptive), and cap-share explains -2 to 72% depending on run, i.e. the decomposition itself varies by more than its signal. The headline statement overstates what a 2-seed, partition-confounded contrast supports.

title: Controls not dose-matched although a dose-matched version was cheap; cross-arm inferences are therefore unfair
quote: takes 3–4× Run A’s optimizer steps
explanation: The no-filter arm trains on 1,400 examples versus 326-440 for filtered, and gold on 350, so the three arms differ in steps, truncation rate (62.4% vs 24.5%) and content. The paper then reports 'no filter is lower on pass@k' in the abstract and Discussion, while asserting that it cannot be attributed. A random subsample of the no-filter pool to the filtered size (or a size-matched random selection) would have been a direct, cheap fix and is exactly the 'check the dose first' protocol the paper recommends in 5.3(iii) to others. Since the same lesson was identified post hoc and deferred to 'first thing next', the claim 'removing the filter makes no consistent difference' is neither a null nor a difference; and a no-filter arm is missing altogether from the final round, where the loop declines.

title: Round-0 baselines and comparisons: untrained rows differ per seed and the gate has one seed against a single baseline
quote: round-0 pass@1 is 49.2, 46.8,
explanation: Round-0 pass@1 differs by 2.4 points between seeds from sampling alone at k=2, a sizeable fraction of the -3.2 to -4.8 effects. The decline of each seed is measured against its own noisy round 0, and the table reports one 'Untrained (seed 1)' row. The gate (-32.2) is one seed, and there is no frozen/untrained re-sampled control (the Xu et al. recommendation cited by the authors) to estimate sampling-only variation at the final-round setting; bootstrap intervals omit this because round-0 draws are treated as fixed. Replicate round-0 draws (cheap: generation only) would give a direct noise-floor for the loop effect and would show whether -4.1 is distinguishable from re-sampling variation.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Revised Recipe

title: Grader and verifier regime differs across arms and rounds, undercutting cross-round comparisons
quote: normalised gold answers, and a pool of 300 problems from
explanation: Earlier runs are graded by V with the gold-storage defect (which rejects 15-18% of correct answers and zeroes 10% of problems), whereas the final round uses normalised gold and a second string-match grader that reads only the last \boxed. It is unclear whether the gold-storage defect and the 51 unparseable golds persist in the final round; if they were fixed, the final-round round-0 accuracy and selection pool are measured differently from every earlier run (round-0 ~49% on 500 vs ~31-33% on 150), so the 'detectable 6 vs 10 points' and the sign-consistent decline are not comparable to the earlier null. Conversely, if not fixed, selection still has the defect. The paper also never reports whether the independent grader agrees with V at the problem level (only differences), so agreement of aggregate deltas is weak evidence of validity.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Revised Recipe

title: Injected-bias interpretations are applied selectively despite being declared uninterpretable
quote: more than in the unbiased seeds, which we do not interpret
explanation: The rule-visible control is a single run with no r_t, and the paper calls both controls invalid. Yet it draws directional conclusions ('a shift in the direction opposite to avoidance', -3.7/-2.7/-5.5 comparison) from an interval [-2.8,+8.3] that includes zero, and declines to interpret a pass@1 drop of 7.0 [-11.2,-3.0] that excludes zero and is larger than in the unbiased seeds. The same standard (n=1, CI) is applied in opposite directions: the non-significant shift is read, the significant one is not. Also the rule affects only 35 of 298 kept examples (263 vs 298), so the intervention is too weak to induce avoidance and cannot discriminate, which is the reason it is not a valid control; reporting the comparison against unbiased seeds adds apparent evidence it cannot carry.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Revised Recipe

title: Audit and Table 5: intervals mostly include zero yet drift in the control arm is used to dismiss; no multiplicity across 15 intervals
quote: so rt drifts as much as the falls we observe, unrelated to the veriﬁer.
explanation: Table 5 reports 15 intervals; the 'all' self-training falls (-2.6,-2.6,-1.5) have intervals touching zero, and the gold arm rises (+3.3,+2.1) with intervals including zero. Claiming that r_t 'drifts as much as the falls' treats non-significant point estimates in a single-seed pair as a baseline and compares them to other non-significant estimates; no contrast (self-training minus gold) with its own interval is given. The identity r_t = r_boxed x boxed share is correct, but it means the audit is designed so the main quantity is largely determined by a non-adaptation variable (boxed share), which the authors acknowledge. The conclusion is therefore sound but the evidence is not an audit with calibrated power, and the proposal is labelled as a 'protocol' despite no demonstration that it can detect anything (no positive control).

title: Unparseable-gold problems and partition differences affect fairness of paired/cross-seed comparisons
quote: 11–18 such problems per exam partition
explanation: V cannot score 7-12% of each 150-problem exam partition, so these problems contribute zero to both rounds and can never be in the pool, limiting headroom and varying by partition (11 to 18). Cross-seed comparisons (A vs B 'flip', replicate gauge, 'seed 2 differs from seed 1') mix partition difficulty, unparseable count and training variance, and the paper does not stratify or restrict to parseable-gold problems, although it offered that analysis (46 of 51 become parseable under V'). The statement that offsets cancel 'only if those problems would not otherwise change, which we did not check' leaves a known, cheap check undone while headline sensitivity depends on it.
source_section: 3.2 The Verifier and Its Directional Bias

title: Gate failure is probably a measurement/format artefact, so it neither validates nor refutes the recipe
quote:
That style carries no \boxed answer, which both graders read,
and a collapse of this size from 300 reference solutions is also what a pipeline
defect would produce.
explanation: The authors themselves note the gold-trained model drops \boxed (1,577 of 1,600 generations in $-style) and both graders score only the last \boxed. A 32-point pass@1 collapse is then exactly what a boxed-only grader yields without any loss of mathematical ability; the 'normalised gold' change (one of seven) is the most plausible cause, and nothing tests it (no boxed-share/answer-extraction fallback, no check of what the gold targets contain, no minimal run with unnormalised gold). A rerun at 2e-5 reaching the same style shows the failure follows the data format, not the rate. Consequently the gate is failing by construction, cannot serve as a positive control for 'the recipe can help', and the paper correctly says it cannot validate, but it then still uses the gate to define the scope of the null ('the null belongs to this recipe'). Also, even a passing gate (SFT on reference solutions) would not establish that SFT on self-generated, verifier-filtered samples can help, since the data distribution and style differ; a positive control closer to the loop (e.g. samples from a stronger model rewritten in the model's own style) is not attempted. Credit: the authors report the failure rather than hiding it.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Revised Recipe

title: Loop decline of about 4 points matches the boxed-share drop; grader cannot separate lost ability from lost formatting
quote:
It reads only
the last \boxed, so a falling boxed share lowers both graders, and it does not
rule out a format artefact in the gate.
explanation: Section 5.3 reports boxed-share falls of roughly 3-5 points in the same recipe (-3.7, -2.7, -5.5 for the unbiased seeds), which is the same size as the pass@1 (-3.2 to -4.8) and sample-accuracy (-2.9 to -5.4) declines. Since correct answers without \boxed score zero under both graders, the whole decline could be produced by a format shift rather than any change in mathematics, and the paper's own identity makes this explicit for r_t. The 'independent' string-match grader adds no independence on this axis (same \boxed extraction, same gold normalisation, same generations); its agreement (-3.6, -2.2, -4.6) shows only that math-verify is not the source, not that the drop is real. The caveat is given for the gate but not applied to the loop headline. A boxed-free answer extractor, or accuracy conditional on a boxed answer being present, is needed.
related_sections: 4.6 A Final Round with a Revised Recipe

title: Seven simultaneous recipe changes (incl. single round, disjoint pool) confound the final round and change what is being tested
quote:
Because no earlier arm improved, we ran one last round with several recipe
changes made at once, aimed at the suspected causes (no ablation of any single
one)
explanation: Completion-only loss, all-linear LoRA, 1,024 cap, normalised gold, a new 300-problem MATH-train pool, k=2, one adapter and LR 1e-4 all change together. Moreover the final round is a single round with selection problems disjoint from the exam, whereas the earlier collapse story (shrinking pool shaped by the biased verifier, selection==eval in Design P) needs multiple rounds and overlap. So the final round cannot confirm or deny any earlier explanation, and a null/negative here is not comparable with Tables 1-3. 'Aimed at suspected causes' is also unsupported: the paper elsewhere says the cause is not identified. Further, the pool of 300 'MATH training split' problems has no overlap check against MATH-500 (stated), which could bias the loop and the gate in either direction, and the paper does not say whether the three seeds redraw the pool.
